q: A company imports a machine. Costs incurred: purchase price Rs 80 lakh, non-refundable import duty Rs 6 lakh, refundable GST Rs 14 lakh, site preparation Rs 3 lakh, staff training on the new machine Rs 2 lakh, and initial operating losses Rs 5 lakh. What is the capitalised cost under Ind AS 16?
o: Rs 89 lakh
Rs 91 lakh
Rs 96 lakh
Rs 103 lakh
why: Purchase price 80 plus non-refundable duty 6 plus site preparation 3 equals Rs 89 lakh. Refundable GST is recoverable, while training costs and initial operating losses are expressly excluded from cost by Ind AS 16.

q: An aircraft costing Rs 500 crore requires a major engine overhaul every 4 years. Management can identify the overhaul element at Rs 60 crore within the purchase price. Under Ind AS 16 componentisation, how should this be treated?
o: Depreciate Rs 60 crore over 4 years and the balance over aircraft life
Capitalise the overhaul element only in year 4 when the work is done
Expense the overhaul when incurred and depreciate Rs 500 crore fully
Provide for the future overhaul cost rateably over the 4 year cycle
why: Ind AS 16 requires each part with a cost significant to the total and a different useful life to be depreciated separately, so the overhaul component runs over 4 years. Ind AS 37 prohibits provisioning for future repair costs because there is no present obligation.

q: A company adopts the revaluation model for a class of buildings. One building has a revaluation surplus of Rs 20 lakh in equity from an earlier year. A fresh valuation shows a decrease of Rs 32 lakh. How is the decrease recognised?
o: Rs 32 lakh charged entirely to profit or loss as an impairment
Rs 32 lakh charged entirely to other comprehensive income
Rs 20 lakh to other comprehensive income and Rs 12 lakh to profit
Rs 12 lakh to other comprehensive income and Rs 20 lakh to profit
why: A revaluation decrease is debited to OCI only to the extent of the existing credit balance in the revaluation surplus for that same asset, being Rs 20 lakh, with the excess Rs 12 lakh going to profit or loss. The surplus of one asset cannot absorb the deficit of another.

q: Under Schedule II to the Companies Act 2013, a company wishes to depreciate a plant over a useful life longer than the indicative life specified in Part C. Which statement is correct?
o: Permitted only with the prior approval of the Central Government
Permitted if justified by technical advice and disclosed in the accounts
Permitted only for continuous process plants and immovable property
Prohibited, since the Schedule II lives are mandatory maximum lives
why: Schedule II permits a different useful life or residual value where justified by technical advice, subject to disclosure of the justification in the financial statements. The lives are indicative rather than an absolute ceiling for most companies.

q: A qualifying asset is funded from general borrowings. Weighted average general borrowings are Rs 200 crore at a weighted average rate of 9 percent, and total borrowing cost incurred is Rs 18 crore. Average expenditure on the asset was Rs 50 crore. What is capitalised under Ind AS 23?
o: Rs 18 crore
Rs 4.5 crore
Rs 9 crore
Nil for general borrowings
why: The capitalisation rate of 9 percent is applied to the average expenditure on the asset, giving Rs 4.5 crore, capped at total borrowing cost incurred. Applying the rate to total borrowings rather than to asset expenditure is the classic error.

q: A decommissioning liability for a plant was initially measured at Rs 40 lakh using a discount rate of 8 percent. The risk-free rate later falls, increasing the liability by Rs 6 lakh. The asset is carried at cost. Under Appendix A to Ind AS 16 principles, the change is:
o: Adjusted against retained earnings as a prior period item
Charged to profit or loss immediately as a finance cost
Added to the carrying amount of the related asset
Recognised in other comprehensive income as a deficit
why: For assets under the cost model, changes in an existing decommissioning liability from revised discount rates or estimated cash flows are added to or deducted from the cost of the related asset. Only the periodic unwinding of discount goes to profit or loss as a finance cost.

q: Which of the following would NOT trigger suspension of borrowing cost capitalisation under Ind AS 23?
o: An extended period in which construction is halted by a labour strike
A prolonged suspension while fresh regulatory approvals are negotiated
An extended stoppage caused by a shortfall in construction funding
A delay that is a necessary part of readying the asset, such as curing
why: Ind AS 23 does not require suspension for delays that are a necessary part of the process of readying the asset, such as curing or awaiting inventory maturation. Extended interruptions in active development for other reasons do require suspension.

q: While auditing CWIP, the auditor notes a project capitalised for 3 years with no physical progress in the last 18 months. Which audit response is most appropriate?
o: Test the balance for impairment under Ind AS 36 and check CWIP ageing
Insist that depreciation be charged on CWIP from the first spend date
Accept the balance since CWIP is not depreciated and carries no risk
Reclassify the whole balance to intangible assets under development
why: Prolonged inactivity is an impairment indicator, and Schedule III requires CWIP ageing plus separate disclosure for projects that are suspended or overdue against the original plan. Depreciation does not begin until the asset is available for use.

q: A cash generating unit has a carrying amount of Rs 900 lakh including allocated goodwill of Rs 100 lakh. Value in use is Rs 700 lakh and fair value less costs of disposal is Rs 650 lakh. How is the impairment loss allocated?
o: Rs 200 lakh allocated pro rata across all assets including goodwill
Rs 250 lakh, with Rs 100 lakh to goodwill and the balance pro rata
Rs 100 lakh to goodwill and Rs 100 lakh pro rata to other assets
Rs 200 lakh pro rata to the other assets, with goodwill left intact
why: Recoverable amount is the higher of value in use Rs 700 lakh and fair value less costs of disposal Rs 650 lakh, so the loss is Rs 200 lakh. Ind AS 36 requires goodwill to be written off first, then the residual allocated pro rata to other assets.

q: Under Schedule II, when a company changes the useful life of an existing asset, the carrying amount as on the date of change is:
o: Restated retrospectively through a prior period adjustment
Depreciated prospectively over the remaining revised useful life
Written off entirely against retained earnings in that year
Recognised as a revaluation adjustment in other comprehensive income
why: A change in useful life is a change in accounting estimate under Ind AS 8, applied prospectively over the remaining revised life. Retrospective restatement applies only to changes in accounting policy or errors.

q: An entity exchanges a machine with carrying amount Rs 30 lakh and fair value Rs 38 lakh for a machine of similar function. The exchange lacks commercial substance. At what amount is the acquired machine recorded?
o: Rs 38 lakh, being the fair value of the asset given up
Rs 30 lakh, being the carrying amount of the asset given up
The fair value of the asset received, if more clearly evident
Rs 34 lakh, the average of carrying amount and fair value
why: Ind AS 16 requires measurement at the carrying amount of the asset given up when the exchange lacks commercial substance or fair value is not reliably measurable, so no gain is recognised. Fair value measurement applies only where commercial substance exists.

q: The auditor is verifying title deeds of immovable property. The company states that original deeds are with a bank as security for a term loan. The most appropriate procedure is:
o: Visit the site, photograph the boundary walls and note the occupier
Accept the management representation letter as sufficient evidence of title
Rely on property tax receipts in the company name as proof of title
Confirm with the bank and inspect the charge registered with the ROC
why: Direct confirmation from the holder combined with inspection of the registered charge provides independent, external evidence of both existence and the encumbrance. Management representations and tax receipts are weak, internally generated or indirect evidence of legal title.

q: Which cost is capitalisable as a directly attributable cost under Ind AS 16?
o: Professional fees for installing and assembling the new machine
Costs of opening a new facility, including the inauguration ceremony
Administration and other general overheads of the finance team
Costs of relocating an existing asset to a more convenient site
why: Installation and assembly costs and related professional fees are directly attributable to bringing the asset to its location and condition for intended use. Ind AS 16 specifically lists opening costs, general overheads and relocation of existing assets as non-capitalisable.

q: A company sells items produced while testing a new plant before it reaches the condition intended by management. Under the current Ind AS 16 requirement, the sale proceeds and the cost of those items are:
o: Netted off against the cost of the plant as testing related costs
Recognised in profit or loss as revenue and cost of items produced
Credited to other comprehensive income until the plant is commissioned
Deferred and released to profit or loss across the plant useful life
why: Proceeds from selling items produced during the testing phase and their cost are recognised in profit or loss rather than deducted from the cost of the asset. The deduction approach reflects the older position that was subsequently amended.

q: Under Schedule II, the useful life prescribed for general plant and machinery not covered by special provisions, used on a single shift basis, is:
o: 5 years
10 years
15 years
20 years for single shift use
why: Part C of Schedule II prescribes 15 years for general plant and machinery on a single shift basis, with extra depreciation for double and triple shift use. The 20 year and 10 year figures apply to other asset categories.

q: A company classifies a building as held for sale on 1 October. Which statement about depreciation is correct?
o: Charged at half rate for the remainder of the financial year
Reversed in full for the year in which classification occurs
Continues to be charged until the date of the actual sale
Ceases from the date of classification as held for sale
why: Once an asset meets the held for sale criteria under Ind AS 105, depreciation ceases from that date and the asset is measured at the lower of carrying amount and fair value less costs to sell. Continuing depreciation to the sale date is the common error.

q: During physical verification of PPE, the auditor finds that management verifies all assets once every three years on a rotational basis. The auditor should:
o: Assess whether the programme is reasonable and test this cycle results
Disclaim an opinion on PPE since no full annual count was performed
Perform a personal full count of all assets in place of management
Insist on a mandatory full verification of every asset every year
why: A phased programme covering all assets over a reasonable interval is acceptable, and CARO requires the auditor to report on whether the programme is reasonable and whether discrepancies were properly dealt with. The auditor tests management verification rather than replacing it.

q: A revalued asset is derecognised on disposal. The revaluation surplus of Rs 15 lakh relating to it stands in equity. Under Ind AS 16 this surplus is:
o: Retained permanently in the revaluation reserve as a capital reserve
Credited again to other comprehensive income on the disposal date
Recycled to profit or loss as part of the gain on the disposal
Transferred directly to retained earnings, bypassing profit or loss
why: Ind AS 16 allows transfer of the revaluation surplus to retained earnings on derecognition, but it is never recycled through profit or loss. Treating it as part of the disposal gain overstates reported profit.
